notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on 1 Kings 15, drawn from the sources searched.

---

## Verses 1–8: The Reign of Abijam (Abijah) over Judah

**v. 1 – "In the eighteenth year of the reign of Jeroboam… Abijam became king of Judah."** The name "Abijam" appears only in Kings; 2 Chronicles 13 consistently calls him "Abijah" (meaning "Yahweh is my father"). Abijam may mean "my father is Yam" — Yam being a Canaanite sea-god. Some commentators suggest he may have started as Abijah (a Yahweh-worshipper) and degenerated into Abijam (a syncretist). Abijam was not Rehoboam's eldest son, but the son of his favourite wife Maacah, whom Rehoboam designated as heir (2 Chronicles 11:22). He was well-matured when he came to the throne, with fourteen wives, twenty-two sons, and sixteen daughters (2 Chronicles 13:21). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/) · [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-15-commentary) · [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html)

**v. 2 – "He reigned in Jerusalem three years. His mother's name was Maacah daughter of Abishalom."** The three-year reign was not three full years but parts of three calendar years (Hebrew reckoning). "Abishalom" is Absalom, David's rebel son. Since chronological considerations make it unlikely Maacah was Absalom's direct daughter, she was probably his granddaughter — the daughter of Tamar (Absalom's only recorded daughter, 2 Samuel 14:27) who married Uriel of Gibeah (2 Chronicles 13:2). In Chronicles she is also called "Micaiah," likely a variant of Maacah. The naming of the queen mother is significant: in Kings, the mother's name is routinely recorded because she exercised enormous influence over her son's religious direction. [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm) · [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html) · [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-15-commentary)

**v. 3 – "Abijam walked in all the sins that his father before him had committed, and his heart was not as fully devoted to the LORD… as the heart of David."** Abijam continued the idolatrous practices introduced by Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:23) and Solomon's later years. The problem was not merely external behaviour but his heart: it was not "wholly devoted" (Hebrew *shalem* — complete, at peace with God). There is an irony here: 2 Chronicles 13 records Abijam delivering a magnificent sermon against Jeroboam's idolatry, proclaiming "God is with us" — yet he tolerated the same or worse idolatries in Judah. Gill notes that Abijam "did profess the true God, and worshipped him, but not wholly, and only, and sincerely." Ellicott observes that Abijam, like Solomon and Rehoboam, "professed to worship Jehovah only as the supreme God of his Pantheon" — a syncretism worse than Jeroboam's mere unauthorised worship of Yahweh. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/) · [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm) · [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html) · [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-15-commentary)

**v. 4 – "Nevertheless, for the sake of David, the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem by raising up a son to succeed him and to make Jerusalem strong."** The "lamp" is a metaphor for the continuation of David's dynasty — a flame not extinguished. The immediate reference is to the birth and succession of godly Asa. But more broadly, "for David's sake" points to the covenant promise of 2 Samuel 7:12–16. Ellicott comments: "In virtue of the continuity of human history, the Divine law always ordains that, in respect of consequences, the good deeds as well as the sins of fathers are 'visited on their children.'" God preserved the dynasty not because of Abijam's character but because of David's faithfulness. Wiseman (quoted in Enduring Word) says: "This is an instance of God blessing the unworthy for the sake of the worthy." [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/) · [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html) · [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm)

**v. 5 – "For David had done what was right… except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite."** This is the only passage in Scripture that explicitly qualifies the praise of David with this exception. Ellicott notes that some ancient manuscripts (the Vatican LXX and others) omit this clause, and he suggests it may have been "a marginal note which has crept into the text, or a comment of the compiler." If original, it demonstrates that David's general faithfulness, despite a catastrophic moral failure, was sufficient for God to honour his line. [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html) · [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-15-commentary)

**vv. 6–7 – "There was war between the houses of Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of Abijam's life."** The chronic hostility between the two kingdoms continued unabated. 2 Chronicles 13 records a major pitched battle in which Abijam's 400,000 men defeated Jeroboam's 800,000. Abijam captured Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron, and Jeroboam never recovered his strength. The "rest of the acts" are said to be written in "the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah" — a now-lost royal archive, not the biblical book of Chronicles. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/) · [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-15-commentary)

**v. 8 – "Abijam rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David, and his son Asa reigned in his place."** Gill notes a mercy here: an evil king receives an honourable burial, and is succeeded by a godly son. Asa is the first king of Judah recorded as "good" — the first of eight good Judean kings (the northern kingdom had none). [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm) · [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-15-commentary)

## Verses 9–15: The Reforms of King Asa

**vv. 9–10 – "In the twentieth year of Jeroboam's reign… Asa became king of Judah, and he reigned forty-one years. His grandmother's name was Maacah."** Asa's forty-one-year reign matched and exceeded David and Solomon, a sign of divine blessing. Maacah is correctly identified here as his *grandmother* (contrast v. 2, where she is called Abijam's "mother"). She was the wife of Rehoboam and mother of Abijam. Despite Abijam's death, she retained the powerful position of *queen mother* (*gebirah*) into Asa's reign — until his reforms forced her removal. Gill observes it is to Asa's commendation that "though he was educated by an idolatrous woman, yet was not corrupted by her as his father was." [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm) · [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html) · [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/)

**v. 11 – "Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as his father David had done."** Unlike his father Abijam (v. 3), Asa's heart matched David's. The Chronicler fills out the picture: Asa commanded Judah to seek the LORD, built fortified cities, enjoyed a decade of peace, and defeated the Ethiopian (Cushite) invasion under Zerah through prayer (2 Chronicles 14–15). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/) · [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-15-commentary)

**v. 12 – "He banished the male shrine prostitutes from the land and removed all the idols that his fathers had made."** These "perverted persons" (KJV "sodomites") were state-sanctioned cult prostitutes associated with Canaanite fertility worship, introduced under Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:24). Abijam had tolerated them; Asa removed them. Gill notes they were either driven out or executed according to Leviticus 20:13. Asa also removed idols made or tolerated by Solomon, Rehoboam, and Abijam. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/) · [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm)

**v. 13 – "He also removed his grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother because she had made a detestable Asherah pole. Asa chopped down the pole and burned it in the Kidron Valley."** The Hebrew word translated "detestable" (*miphletzeth*) means something "horrible," "frightful," or "abominable." Ellicott and others identify it as an obscene object — likely a phallic emblem associated with Asherah fertility worship, more extreme than the usual wooden Asherah pole. Maacah had apparently presided over its cult. Asa's public burning of the idol in the Kidron Valley (Jerusalem's rubbish dump) and the degradation of his own grandmother "demonstrates the thoroughness of Asa's reforms." Knapp comments: "It is in a man's own family circle that his faithfulness is put fairly to the test." [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/) · [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html) · [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm)

**v. 14 – "The high places were not removed, but Asa's heart was fully devoted to the LORD all his days."** This presents an apparent contradiction with 2 Chronicles 14:3, 5, which say Asa *did* remove the high places. The resolution offered by Enduring Word, Gill, and others: Asa removed the high places dedicated to foreign idols, but not the ones where Yahweh was worshipped (which should also have been removed once the temple was established). Ellicott notes that "the craving for local and visible sanctuaries… proved too strong for even earnest reformers." The critical statement is the second half: despite this imperfection, Asa's heart was "fully devoted" (Hebrew *shalem*, same word used of the ideal in v. 3). This is an important theological point: a "perfect" or "wholly devoted" heart does not mean sinless perfection but sincere, undivided loyalty to Yahweh as the only God. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/) · [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm) · [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html) · [desiringgod.org](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/why-good-men-fail-god)

**v. 15 – "He brought into the house of the LORD the silver and gold and other articles that he and his father had dedicated."** These were spoils of war: Abijam's plunder from his victory over Jeroboam (2 Chronicles 13:19) and Asa's spoils from defeating the Ethiopians (2 Chronicles 14:13). Abijam had devoted items to religious use but died before fulfilling his vows; Asa completed what his father had vowed. This replenished the temple treasury, which had been emptied by Shishak's invasion in Rehoboam's day (1 Kings 14:26). [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm) · [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html)

## Verses 16–24: Asa's War with Baasha and His Decline

**v. 16 – "There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel throughout their days."** Baasha reigned from Asa's 3rd to 27th year. The first ten years of Asa's reign were peaceful (2 Chronicles 14:1); open war erupted later. The phrase "throughout their days" means hostile relations persisted as long as both lived. [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html) · [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm)

**v. 17 – "Baasha… fortified Ramah to prevent anyone from leaving or entering the territory of Asa king of Judah."** Ramah was a Benjaminite city about five miles north of Jerusalem, on the main route between the two kingdoms. Baasha's fortification was a blockade — "a standing menace to Judah" (Ellicott). It was designed to stop the flow of northerners defecting to Judah (2 Chronicles 15:9 records many from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon migrating south during Asa's prosperity) and to exert economic and military pressure. [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html) · [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/) · [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm)

**v. 18 – "So Asa withdrew all the silver and gold that remained in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace… and sent them to Ben-hadad… king of Aram."** This was the critical failure of Asa's reign. Instead of crying out to God as he had against the Ethiopians, he emptied the temple treasury to bribe a pagan king. Poole (quoted in Enduring Word) lists three great faults: (1) alienating consecrated things without necessity; (2) acting out of carnal fear and distrust of God whose power he had already experienced; (3) hiring Ben-hadad to break his existing covenant with Baasha — effectively hiring a pagan to sin. Ben-hadad was the grandson of Hezion (likely the Rezon of 1 Kings 11:23), ruling a Syria that was already rising as a formidable power. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/) · [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm) · [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html)

**v. 19 – "Let there be a treaty between me and you… See, I have sent you a gift of silver and gold. Now go and break your treaty with Baasha."** Asa appealed to an older treaty between his father (Abijam) and Ben-hadad's father (Tabrimmon). He asked Ben-hadad to break a newer treaty with Baasha in exchange for temple treasure. John Piper (Desiring God) observes: "So many times when we rely on ourselves and our own resources, things seem to go well for a season. But things are not well when we have stopped hoping in God and started hoping in what man can do." [desiringgod.org](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/asas-folly) · [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/)

**v. 20 – "Ben-hadad… sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel, conquering Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and the whole land of Naphtali, including the region of Chinnereth."** These were northern territories of Israel, nearest to Syria. Ijon was near Dan at the Jordan's source; Abel-beth-maacah ("meadow of the house of Maacah") lay in marshy ground near the waters of Merom; Chinnereth (later Gennesaret) was the region around the Sea of Galilee. All lay exposed to invasion from the north through Coele-Syria (the valley between Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon). [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html) · [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm)

**v. 21 – "When Baasha learned of this, he stopped fortifying Ramah and withdrew to Tirzah."** Baasha abandoned his Judean campaign to defend his northern border. Tirzah was Israel's capital at the time, in the tribe of Manasseh, closer to the Syrian threat. Syria appears to have retained its northern conquests and some supremacy over Israel until the time of Ahab (see 1 Kings 20:34). [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html)

**v. 22 – "Then King Asa summoned all the men of Judah, with no exceptions, and they carried away the stones of Ramah… and with these materials King Asa built up Geba of Benjamin, as well as Mizpah."** Asa conscripted every available man — Jewish tradition says even newlyweds exempted from military service and students of the wise were called up. He dismantled Baasha's fortification and used the materials to fortify Geba (north of Jerusalem, on the edge of a valley) and Mizpah (on the ridge continuing from the Mount of Olives). These became the new northern outposts of Judah. [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm) · [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html)

**v. 23 – "In his old age, however, he became diseased in his feet."** 2 Chronicles 16:12 fills this out: in the 39th year of his reign, Asa developed a severe foot disease and "did not seek the LORD, but the physicians." Commentators generally identify the disease as gout (the traditional Jewish view, noted by Gill), though Wiseman suggests it was more likely "peripheral obstructive vascular disease with ensuing gangrene" given its severity and Asa's death within two years. The Chronicler's criticism is not that Asa consulted physicians per se, but that he trusted in them *instead of* the LORD — possibly Egyptian physicians who used charms, incantations, and magical arts. The Hebrew construction (2 Chronicles 16:12) implies superstitious trust, not mere medical consultation. This failure of faith echoes his earlier treaty with Syria. Ellicott notes: "Prosperity, it is implied, had somewhat deteriorated his character." [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm) · [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html) · [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/) · [studylight.org (Keil & Delitzsch on 2 Chron 16:12)](https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/16-12.html)

**v. 24 – "Asa rested with his fathers… and his son Jehoshaphat reigned in his place."** Despite the sad decline, Asa received an honourable burial with great pomp — laid on a bed filled with sweet odours and spices, and a great fire was made in his honour (2 Chronicles 16:14). His son Jehoshaphat was a godly successor. Some scholars hold that Jehoshaphat became coregent during Asa's final years of illness (c. 873–870 BC). Morgan's assessment: "It is the record of a faulty life, but one in which the deepest thing, that of desire, was right; and so it is the record of a life, the influence of which was a blessing rather than a curse." [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/) · [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm) · [studylight.org (Constable)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-15.html)

## Verses 25–32: The Reign of Nadab and the Fall of Jeroboam's Dynasty

**v. 25 – "In the second year of Asa's reign… Nadab son of Jeroboam became king of Israel, and he reigned two years."** Nadab's two years were not two full years — he began in Asa's second year and was assassinated in Asa's third year, so his reign spanned parts of two calendar years (perhaps little more than one actual year). [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm) · [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/)

**v. 26 – "He did evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of his father and in his sin, which he had caused Israel to commit."** Nadab perpetuated Jeroboam's calf-worship at Bethel and Dan. 2 Chronicles 11:14 adds that Jeroboam and his sons drove God's priests out of Israel. Knapp notes: "Nadab's name means *willing*; and he appears to have been too willing to continue in, and perpetuate, the sin of his iniquitous father." [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/) · [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-15-commentary)

**v. 27 – "Baasha son of Ahijah of the house of Issachar conspired against Nadab, and Baasha struck him down at Gibbethon of the Philistines."** Gibbethon was a Levitical city in the territory of Dan (Joshua 19:44; 21:23). It had apparently fallen into Philistine hands during Israel's decline. Nadab was besieging it when Baasha, likely a military officer in Nadab's army, assassinated him. Ellicott notes that the siege must have been fruitless — twenty-six years later, Gibbethon was still in Philistine hands (1 Kings 16:15). Baasha, from the obscure tribe of Issachar and of low origin (1 Kings 16:2), is "the first of the many military chiefs who by violence or assassination seized upon the throne of Israel." [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html) · [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm) · [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/)

**vv. 28–29 – "In the third year of Asa… Baasha killed Nadab and reigned in his place… he struck down the entire household of Jeroboam… according to the word that the LORD had spoken through… Ahijah the Shilonite."** This fulfilled the prophecy of 1 Kings 14:10–14 — that every male of Jeroboam's house would be cut off and none would receive burial. Yet Baasha did not act from pious motives; he was an ambitious usurper. Clarke observes: "Thus God made use of one wicked man to destroy another." Ellicott adds: "Sin which works out God's purpose is not the less truly sin" — a point confirmed in 1 Kings 16:7, where God judges Baasha in part *because* he killed Jeroboam's house. Had Jeroboam remained obedient, God had promised him a lasting dynasty (1 Kings 11:38). Instead, his dynasty lasted just two generations — the first of nine dynasties that would rule (or misrule) Israel in 250 years. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/) · [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html) · [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm)

**v. 30 – "Because of the sins Jeroboam had committed and had caused Israel to commit… he had provoked the LORD… to anger."** This verse gives the theological reason for the judgment, distinct from Baasha's political motives. Jeroboam's sin was not merely personal — he "caused Israel to commit" it, instituting a system of idolatrous worship that would plague the northern kingdom for its entire history. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/)

**vv. 31–32 – "As for the rest of the acts of Nadab… are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? And there was war between Asa and Baasha… throughout their days."** The formulaic closing. The "Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel" was the northern kingdom's royal archive, distinct from the biblical Chronicles. The war between Asa and Baasha is the same conflict described in vv. 16–22. [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm)

## Verses 33–34: The Reign of Baasha over Israel

**vv. 33–34 – "In the third year of Asa's reign… Baasha son of Ahijah became king of all Israel, and he reigned in Tirzah twenty-four years. And Baasha did evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of Jeroboam."** Baasha's twenty-four-year reign matched the combined length of Jeroboam and Nadab. Though not a genetic descendant of Jeroboam, he was his spiritual heir — perpetuating the same calf-worship and idolatry. Baasha came to power through bloody assassination and ruled wickedly. The contrast between the turbulent, short-lived dynasties of the north and the stable Davidic dynasty of the south (sustained by God's covenant promise) is a major theological theme of Kings. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/) · [biblehub.com (Gill)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/15.htm) · [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html)

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**Reformed / Baptist (Desiring God / John Piper) on Asa's failure (vv. 16–20):** Piper emphasises God's sovereign searching — "the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to show Himself strong on behalf of those whose heart is loyal to Him" (2 Chronicles 16:9). Asa's folly was not merely a tactical mistake; it was unbelief that robbed him of greater blessing. God would have given Syria itself into Asa's hand had he trusted. Failure came because Asa treated this as a "smaller trouble" he could manage by human means. The lesson is that even good men can fail God when they stop trusting. [desiringgod.org](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/asas-folly) · [desiringgod.org](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/why-good-men-fail-god)

**Reformed / Baptist (Spurgeon, via Enduring Word on 2 Chron 16):** Spurgeon speculated that Asa resorted to human help precisely because this was a *smaller* trouble than the Ethiopian invasion: "In the case of the invasion by countless hordes of Ethiopians, Asa must have felt that it was of no use calling in Ben-hadad… therefore he was driven to God. But this being a smaller trial, he does not seem to have been so thoroughly divorced from confidence in man." A warning that we often trust God for "big" things but rely on ourselves for "smaller" ones. [enduringword.com (2 Chron 16)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-16/)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Guzik treats Asa's foot disease (v. 23) partly as "personal discipline for his trust in the flesh," while also emphasising the supernatural dimension of Asa's earlier victory over the Ethiopians through prayer. There is a strong emphasis on the need for lifelong faithfulness — Asa "did not finish well." The possibility of divine healing is implicit in the critique that Asa "did not seek the LORD, but the physicians." [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-15/)

**Lutheran, Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott's approach is measured and historical-critical, noting textual variants (e.g., v. 5 possibly being a later marginal note, v. 6 a possible textual error). He is cautious about the relationship between the Chronicler and Kings, noting harmonisation difficulties (the high places, the dating of Baasha's attack). He reads Asa's appeal to Syria as a serious moral failure that "deserved and received prophetic rebuke" — calling in a heathen power against "brethren, the children of Israel." [studylight.org (Ellicott)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-15.html)

**Wesleyan / Methodist (Wesley's Notes):** John Wesley's Explanatory Notes (linked but not fully retrieved) would characteristically emphasise the practical and holiness dimensions — Asa's reforms as a model of righteous action and his later failures as warnings against backsliding. The Wesleyan tradition highlights that a "perfect heart" (v. 14) means sincere and complete devotion, not sinless flawlessness — consonant with the Wesleyan doctrine of Christian perfection as purity of intention.

---

## Other Views

**Catholic reading (traditional):** The Catholic tradition would see the Davidic "lamp" (v. 4) as a type of Christ and the perpetual dynasty fulfilled in Jesus. Asa's removal of the queen mother and destruction of the Asherah pole would be read as upholding the first commandment against idolatry and the necessity of reforming even family relationships for the sake of truth — themes consistent with Catholic social teaching on the primacy of God. **Modern scholarship (textual issues):** Ellicott flags several textual questions — the omission of "except in the matter of Uriah" (v. 5) in the Vatican LXX; the apparent awkward repetition in v. 6; and the chronological difficulty in v. 17, where the Chronicler's "thirty-sixth year of Asa" does not align with Baasha's known reign (he died in Asa's 27th year). Some scholars resolve this by reading "thirty-sixth year" as counting from the division of the kingdom rather than Asa's personal reign — i.e., the 16th year of Asa himself. **The name "Abijam" vs. "Abijah" (Dilday, via Precept Austin):** Some modern scholars suggest the Kings writer deliberately uses Abijam ("my father is Yam," a Canaanite sea-god) instead of Abijah ("Yahweh is my father") as a theological judgment — the king who preached Yahweh but tolerated idolatry is subtly branded with the name of a Canaanite deity. Matthew 1:7 retains the positive form "Abijah" in Christ's genealogy.
